query: For refractory high-entropy alloys intended for structural use under extreme-temperature conditions, what single intervention could improve high-temperature oxygen resistance? State one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to the untreated alloy, defines the temperature, atmosphere, and exposure conditions under which it should work, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment with a clear result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a small fraction of aluminum (e.g., ~5 at.%) to a baseline refractory high-entropy alloy will improve its high-temperature oxidation resistance by forming a stable alumina (Al2O3) scale that suppresses oxygen ingress.
generation.material_initial_state: A conventional refractory high-entropy alloy with minimal or no aluminum content (e.g., MoNbTaW(V) composition).
generation.intervention: Introduce ~5 at.% aluminum to the alloy during vacuum induction melting.
generation.conditions: Air exposure at ~1200°C for at least 50 hours under ambient pressure conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: Stable and continuous Al2O3 scale formed on the alloy surface.
generation.mechanism: Aluminum additions preferentially form a dense, adherent alumina layer that slows further oxidation of the refractory elements and protects the underlying matrix from rapid oxygen diffusion.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the untreated base alloy, the Al-doped alloy will exhibit a significantly reduced mass gain (e.g., by 30–50%) over 50 hours of oxidation testing.
generation.baseline: Without aluminum additions, the refractory alloy forms less protective oxide layers that lead to higher scale spallation and mass gain at elevated temperatures.
generation.boundary: At temperatures above ~1300°C or at extremely long exposure times, the alumina scale can degrade or spall, decreasing its protective effect. Also, the exact magnitude of improvement may vary with alloy composition and microstructure.
generation.uncertainty: Exact quantitative improvements for very long exposures or higher temperatures are not fully validated by current data.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: baseline alloy and ~5 at.% Al-modified alloy, both processed similarly by vacuum induction melting. Subject both sets to isothermal oxidation in air at 1200°C for 50 hours.
measurements: Mass gain or oxide scale thickness measurements every 10 hours
Microstructural characterization (SEM/EDS) of the oxide layer after exposure
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If aluminum doping does not lower mass gain or produce a more protective alumina-based oxide scale compared to the baseline, then the hypothesis is falsified.

Research has proved that RHEAs have excellent mechanical properties at high temperatures, even surpassing the widely used nickel-based alloy [ [2] , [3] , [4] , [5] , [6] ]. Refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) are considered to be a new generation of high-temperature materials, because they have the advantages of both high-entropy alloys (HEAs) and refractory metals (RMs), such as high-temperature strength, high hardness, and good phase stability at high temperatures [ [1] , [2] , [3] , [4] , [5] , [6] , [7] ]. They are mainly composed of Mo, Nb, Ta, and W, while Ti, Cr, V, Si, and Al are usually used as strengthening alloy elements [ [8] , [9] , [10] , [11] , [12] , [13] , [14] ]. For example, Mo 25 Nb 25 Ta 25 W 25 and Mo 20 Nb 20 Ta 20 W 20 V 20 are two of the types of most extensively studied RHEAs [ [7] ]. The neutron diffraction analysis of those alloys after annealing at 1400 °C for 19 h shows that no changes have occurred to their phase structures. Their compression yield strengths are much higher than that of Inconel 718 alloy at temperatures above 800 °C. Furthermore, their yield strengths are still higher than 500 MPa at 1200 °C [ [15] , [16] ]. chosen.lever: Al content in the alloy composition
chosen.technique: Vacuum induction melting with controlled aluminum additions
chosen.conditions: High-temperature oxidation experiments conducted above 1200°C in air
chosen.why: Adding Al is a well-known and direct approach to enhance high-temperature oxidation resistance in refractory high-entropy alloys, as Al2O3 provides a stable and adherent oxide layer. Prior research shows that Al-containing superalloys form protective scales in oxidizing atmospheres at elevated temperatures. A systematic oxidation experiment, comparing Al-doped versus undoped alloys under the same high-temperature air exposure, would clearly test whether the Al addition improves oxidation resistance. If no protective alumina scale forms or no improvement in weight gain suppression is observed, the hypothesis that Al doping is responsible for enhanced oxidation resistance would be falsified.
